sections.html:
The toadfishes comprise about 73 species in around 22 genera and three subfamilies. One subfamily, the Thalassophryninae, is known as the "venomous toadfishes". Thalassophryne amazonica, one of the very few freshwater species of the family, belongs to it.

The Amazon Toadfish can easily be told apart from all other toadfishes in South and Central America: it is the only species in which the dorsal, caudal and anal fins are connected with each other. Although a few other Thalassophryninae occasionally enter brackish and fresh water, Thalassophryne amazonica is the only species of the subfamily that lives exclusively in fresh water.
They need a sandy bottom in which they can burrow. Maximum length is about 8-10 cm.
The fish are fed with small feeder fishes.

Against each other and any other fish that does not serve as food, Thalassophryne amazonica are very peaceful. Because toadfish do not move unnecessarily, they can be kept in comparatively small aquaria.
Toadfish are said to care for the brood, but no details have been published so far.

The Thalassophryninae are thought to have the most highly developed venomous apparatus of all fishes. The venom glands are located at the base of two hollow spines (derived from dorsal fin spines) on the back and two additional spines on the operculum.

There are no reports of accidents with Thalassophryne amazonica, but each year several cases occur with the closely related marine and brackish species Thalassophryne nattereri, which is very abundant in Brazil. The sting causes strong pain, inflammation and sometimes necrosis, but the venom apparently has no systemic components. There are no reports of fatalities.

Etymology: Thalassophryne means "sea-toad"; amazonica means "coming from the Amazon"; nattereri honours the naturalist Johann Natterer (1787-1843).
